newsitem.title: MOROCCO: World Bank urges Morocco to speed up economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: World Bank urges Morocco to speed up economic reforms.

text.p: Morocco should speed up its economic and social reforms to ensure a sustainable annual growth of 5.0 to 6.0 percent of gross domestic product and reduce social disparities, the World Bank said.

The Bank, in a 60-page report obtained by Reuters on Friday, said: "The next three years will be decisive for Morocco to set up conditions for a sustained futur development...But Morocco can meet the target of an annual 5.0 to 6.0 percent growth of GDP on condition it speeds up its vast reform programme."
In the last 10 years, the country has made great steps towards transforming its economy, to good growth and stability of its macro-economic indicators, the Bank said in the report issued last month.

"But the economy remains extremely sensitive to drought and is too little diversified. The fundamental elements of growth are inadequate as is shown by weak saving and investment rates," the report said.

Morocco's economy posted a growth of 11.8 percent in 1996 and would register between 3.0 to 4.0 percent growth in 1997, Finance Ministry Mohamed Kabbaj recently said. He said national saving rose to 19 percent of GDP against 16 percent in 1995.
But investment dropped to 20.5 percent in 1996, from 22 percent in 1996, he said.
"Morocco also needs to reduce the unemployment and rural poverty," the Bank's report said.

Urban unemployment is estimated at 18.5 percent in 1996 and according to the Statistics Directorate, an estimated 13 percent of Morocco's 27 million inhabitants live below the poverty line and earn around $300 per year.
Morocco's GDP reached 316 billion dirhams ($34.3 billion) in 1996, or an average $1,300 per head.
"The macro-economic equilibrium remains precarious and debt remains a serious issue," the Bank said.
Morocco's total debt is estimated at $21 billion of which the Treasury holds a stake of $14 billion. It represented 60 percent of GDP in 1996 against 68 percent in 1995, Kabbaj has said.
Kabbaj forecast that the debt would drop to 40 percent of GDP by the year 2000.
